opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's one of the most important things we've done. Designing a chip is a long process. From when you start a design to when it's deployed in a data center is maybe two to three years, and then that chip has to stay useful for another several years. So you're really trying to predict where machine learning will be somewhere between two and six years out, and that's a field that changes enormously over that kind of horizon.

If hardware designers work in isolation, they'll optimize for today's workloads, and by the time the chip ships, the models may look quite different. Having ML researchers in the room helps you make better bets. Researchers can say, "We're seeing interesting results with lower-precision arithmetic," or "Sparsity and mixture-of-experts style models seem to be getting more important," or "Memory bandwidth, not raw compute, is going to be the bottleneck for inference on these larger models." Those signals shape decisions about numeric formats, how much on-chip memory you include, how the interconnect between chips is designed, and so on.

It also works the other way. When researchers understand what the hardware does well and what's expensive, they can design models that map efficiently onto it. Some of the gains we've seen came less from the hardware or the models alone and more from co-designing the two. You get multiplicative benefits when the algorithm, the software stack and compilers, and the silicon all evolve together.

Also, not every bet has to pay off. You can include some features that might matter a lot if a research direction takes off, and accept that some won't get heavily used. Making those calls well depends on close, ongoing conversation between the people building chips and the people building models.

r001.rationale: The response says chip design and deployment take two to three years, followed by several years of use, so designers must predict where machine learning will be two to six years ahead.

r002.rationale: It explains that research signals such as lower precision, sparsity, and memory bottlenecks shape hardware decisions, including numeric formats, on-chip memory, and interconnect design.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the fundamental issue is that hardware design has these very long lead times. If you're starting to design a chip today, it's probably going to be fabricated and deployed in data centers something like two to three years from now, and then it's going to be in service for another three to five years after that. So you're really trying to predict what machine learning researchers are going to want to do five or six years out, and that's a pretty hard thing to do, because the field moves incredibly fast.

So the way we've approached it is to have the chip architects and the ML researchers in the same room, really. The researchers can say, here are the kinds of models we think are going to matter, here's where we think the computational bottlenecks are heading, maybe sparsity is going to be more important, maybe lower precision is going to be fine for these kinds of workloads. And the hardware people can push back and say, well, if you did it this way instead, we could make it ten times more efficient. That back and forth is really valuable, because often the researchers don't realize that a small change in how they formulate a problem could make it dramatically cheaper on hardware, and the chip designers don't necessarily know which flexibility actually matters and which is just baggage.

One concrete example from the early TPU work was the realization that for inference, you really didn't need 32-bit floating point. Eight-bit integer arithmetic was good enough for a lot of the models we cared about, and that let us pack far more compute into the same silicon area and power budget. That's not a decision a chip designer would make in isolation, and it's not one a researcher would make in isolation either. It came from the two groups understanding each other's constraints.

And I think that's only going to get more important going forward. As models get larger and more expensive to train and serve, the co-design of the algorithms, the software stack, the compilers, and the hardware is where a lot of the efficiency gains are going to come from. You can't really optimize any one of those layers independently anymore.

r001.rationale: The response says hardware lead times mean predicting researchers’ needs five or six years out, supported by a two-to-three-year deployment timeline and several more years in service.

r002.rationale: It explains that researchers’ expected models and computational bottlenecks—including sparsity and lower precision—influence hardware design choices, with an early TPU example.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s important because you’re designing hardware for what machine learning will need several years from now, and that’s a moving target. The chip designers need to understand where the research is heading: what kinds of computations we’ll want to do, how much memory they’ll need, and how much communication there will be between chips.

And it goes the other way, too. Researchers benefit from understanding which operations are inexpensive in hardware and which are really costly. Sometimes a small change to an algorithm can make it much more efficient without compromising the result.

So you want a close feedback loop. If you design hardware solely around today’s models, you risk having a very efficient chip for a workload that has changed by the time the chip is ready. Having researchers and hardware designers work together helps you balance efficiency with enough flexibility to support what comes next.

r001.rationale: It says hardware is designed for ML needs “several years from now” and mentions anticipating future computations.

r002.rationale: It says chip designers need to understand where research is heading and use that to guide future hardware design.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think it’s important because the hardware and the algorithms really influence each other. As machine learning researchers, we can give chip designers a sense of what kinds of computations are likely to matter in the future, where the bottlenecks are, and which numerical precisions we can tolerate. Those choices can have a pretty dramatic effect on performance and energy efficiency.

And it goes the other way, too. If hardware designers tell us that a particular kind of operation or data movement is expensive, we can sometimes change the model or the algorithm to accomplish the same thing in a much more hardware-friendly way.

The challenge is that designing a chip takes years, while machine learning moves very quickly. So you want that ongoing conversation to help distinguish the properties that are likely to persist from the details of whatever model happens to be popular today.

r001.rationale: The response says chip design takes years and that designers should anticipate what computations will matter, but it gives no roughly two-to-six-year time horizon.

r002.rationale: It explains that researchers’ forecasts about important computations, bottlenecks, and tolerable numerical precision guide chip designers’ choices for future hardware, including TPUs in the preceding context.
